title: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions
competency: Explain conduction and electrolytic cells, predict preferential discharge and write electrode reactions for common electrolyses.

keywords.def: Conduction by moving ions in a molten or dissolved electrolyte, with a chemical change.
Decomposing a molten or dissolved ionic compound by passing a direct current through it.
When several ions reach an electrode, only one kind is discharged.
An electrode (graphite, platinum) that only carries electrons and does not react.
An electrode (Cu, Ag, Ni) that takes part; as an anode it dissolves.
A concentrated solution of sodium chloride in water.

en.text: Metals conduct by moving electrons: no matter moves and no chemical change happens, and conductivity falls as temperature rises. Electrolytes conduct by moving ions, only when molten or dissolved: matter moves, chemical changes happen at the electrodes, and conductivity rises with temperature.

en.text: In electrolysis a direct current decomposes a molten or dissolved ionic compound. Cations move to the cathode (negative electrode) and are reduced; anions move to the anode (positive electrode) and are oxidized. Molten NaCl gives sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

screens.after: Opposite charges attract: Na⁺ goes to the negative cathode, Cl⁻ to the positive anode.

en.text: When more than one kind of ion reaches an electrode, only one is discharged. It depends on (1) the position of the ion in the electrochemical series (lower is discharged first), (2) its concentration (a very concentrated ion can win), and (3) the electrode: an active anode such as copper dissolves instead of any anion being discharged.

screens.title: Brine at the cathode
screens.ask: In brine, Na⁺ and H⁺ both reach the cathode. Which is discharged?
screens.after: H⁺ (from water) is much easier to reduce than Na⁺, so H₂ forms.

screens.title: Three factors
paras: 1. Position: the ion lower in the electrochemical series is discharged first.
2. Concentration: a much more concentrated ion can be discharged first.
3. Electrode: inert (graphite, Pt) or active (Cu, Ag, Ni).

screens.title: Displacing metals
paras: A metal displaces ions of metals below it in the reactivity series.
Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, but Ag cannot displace Cu²⁺.
Metals above H displace H₂ from acids.

screens.text: Why does brine give Cl₂ at the anode while dilute NaCl gives O₂?
opts: Cl⁻ is lower than OH⁻ in the series
screens.why: OH⁻ is slightly easier to discharge, but a very high [Cl⁻] wins.
screens.clue: Which of the three factors changes?

en.text: In water, H⁺/H₂O and OH⁻/H₂O compete with the salt's ions. Brine gives H₂, Cl₂ and leaves NaOH. Dilute NaCl, dilute H₂SO₄ and NaOH all just decompose water into H₂ and O₂ (2 : 1 by volume). CuSO₄ with inert electrodes gives Cu and O₂ and turns acidic; with copper electrodes copper simply moves from anode to cathode.

am.text: ጨዋማ ውሃ H₂፣ Cl₂ ይሰጣል NaOH ይቀራል። የተቀጠነ NaCl፣ H₂SO₄ እና NaOH ውሃን ወደ H₂ እና O₂ ይከፍላሉ።

notes.text: p.74: electrolysis is defined only "in aqueous solution"; molten compounds are electrolyzed too (Figure 2.3).
p.75–76: the −0.83 V value is for 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; the book's overall brine equation (2H⁺ + 2Cl⁻ → H₂ + Cl₂) does not show the OH⁻ build-up. "compute" should be "compete".
p.78: overall reaction should be 2H₂O(l), not H₂O(g); CuSO₄ dissociates into Cu²⁺, not "Cu⁺". Table 2.1 "forms hydroxides" is true only for the first group.
The outcomes mention Ni electrodes for CuSO₄, but the text treats only inert and copper electrodes.
